sections.html:
Tallapoosa County lies in the Piedmont of east-central Alabama. Dadeville is the seat and Alexander City the largest city. The Tallapoosa River winds through, and the county's website boasts more than 850 miles of shoreline. Waterfront homes are valued differently from inland lots; if you own one, find out how the revenue office appraised the land and the buildings.

U.S. 280, which doubles as State Route 38, is the big federal road, with state routes 14, 22, 49, 50, 63, 120, 128 and 259 filling in. Buyers will not find an interstate here, so tie your listing to the closest highway and the closest town.

The 2020 count was 41,311 people, 17,376 households and 22,686 housing units. The 2025 estimate is 40,953, a slow drift down from 41,616 in 2010. Almost a quarter of housing units were vacant. Some of those are second homes or units between occupants, so an empty house on your street does not prove a weak market.

Housing measureTallapoosa County
Housing units (2020)22,686
Vacant units23.4%
Owner-occupied share71.3%
Renter-occupied share28.7%
Homeowner vacancy rate1.7%
Rental vacancy rate9.0%
Residents in rural areas78.4%

With 78.4 percent of residents in rural areas, many sales involve acreage, outbuildings or private water and septic.

Three cities, Alexander City, Dadeville and Tallassee, share the county with the towns of Camp Hill, Daviston, Goldville, Jackson's Gap and New Site. Tallassee spills over into Elmore County. Alexander City Schools, Tallapoosa County Schools and the Tallassee City School District serve the county.

Three districts mean the school boundary can change from one road to the next. Families shopping by school zone will want the answer, so confirm your district first. Some buyers also search by community name, such as Andrew Jackson, Cherokee Bluffs, Church Hill or Dudleyville, so use that name in your listing details when it applies.

Here the state calendar applies. October 1 is the due date, and a bill left unpaid past December 31 becomes delinquent, picking up penalties and interest as it ages.

Phone the revenue office ahead of choosing a closing date, and have the payoff put on paper for whoever handles the closing. Useful things to ask:

  • What is owed for the current year, and for any earlier year?
  • Is the bill in the previous owner's name?
  • Which exemptions are on the parcel today?

File a written protest with the County Board of Equalization within 30 days of the written notice of valuation. State law sets that window in Code of Alabama sections 40-3-20, 40-3-24 and 40-3-25. The county sets its own hearing dates and forms, so call the office.

Believe the number is inflated? Show up with an appraisal, contractor bids or sales of similar houses nearby. Dated photos of a sagging porch or a bad roof carry more weight than opinions. Keep a copy of everything you hand over, and note the date you mailed or delivered it.

Back tax does not stop a sale. At closing the title company sends the county its share from your proceeds, which makes an accurate payoff figure the main job. Request it from the county, include any older balance, and give the total to the closing agent so nothing is missed.

If the house is an inherited one, expect the title company to want proof of who may sign. Bring the death certificate and any court papers. Heirs who live out of state can usually sign by mail or before a notary.

sections.h2: How a cash sale works here
sections.html:
A cash sale follows the same steps as any Alabama sale, minus the lender. You send details about the house and receive a written offer. If it suits you, you pick a closing date, and a title company clears any lien and tax balance from the proceeds.

That path can help when a house has deferred repairs, a lapsed tenant or heirs who live out of state. It also removes the wait for a lender's appraisal, which matters when a house needs work that a loan appraiser might flag.

sections.h2: Step by step: from decision to closing
sections.html:
First, decide how you want to sell: list with an agent, or ask a cash buyer for an offer. Second, collect the paperwork. Third, get the tax payoff. Fourth, review the offer or contract and confirm who pays the current year's tax. Fifth, the title company searches the record, resolves anything it finds and schedules the signing. Last, the deed is recorded and the money reaches you.

Most holdups arrive at steps three and five, and the cure is simply to begin them sooner than feels necessary. Heirs who have not agreed, an old lien nobody remembered or a tax bill in a dead parent's name can each add weeks. A payoff request costs nothing, and it clears away the most common snag. Ask the title company to tell you at the start what they need from you, so you can send it all in one batch and avoid repeated calls.

Pull together the deed, the latest tax statement, any protest letters, receipts for major repairs and the names of everyone on the title. For a lakeside or rural parcel, add the survey, septic records and any easement papers. Tidy records mean fewer buyer questions and a faster close.

If tenants live in the house, give them notice before showings begin and keep a copy of the lease handy for buyers who ask about rent and term. A lapsed tenant or a vacant unit is easier to sell when the condition is documented with dated photos.

Waterfront and acreage parcels behave differently in a sale. Buyers want to know about shoreline rights, dock permits, flood exposure, the water source and the septic system. Ask the revenue office how the land and the improvements were valued separately, because a dock, boathouse or outbuilding can be a line of its own on the assessment.

Insurance quotes matter too. A buyer's lender may require flood or wind coverage, and a high quote can reduce what a buyer is willing to pay. Having a recent quote in hand lets you answer that question before it becomes a negotiation point.

The median age is 46.4, and 22.5 percent of residents were 65 or older in 2020, so estate sales and downsizing come up often. A given street may differ from the county as a whole.

  • Estate and heir sales, especially where a parent owned the house for decades.
  • Rental houses, in a market with a 9.0 percent rental vacancy rate.
  • Rural parcels that need survey, access or septic answers before closing.
  • Houses held by older owners who are ready to move closer to family.

Tallapoosa County sits alone in the Alexander City micropolitan area, which only changes how federal data is grouped. It does not change how your house is taxed or sold.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Tallapoosa County?
faqs.a: October 1, and they are delinquent after December 31.

faqs.q: Where is the Tallapoosa County seat?
faqs.a: Dadeville. The largest city is Alexander City.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal a Tallapoosa County value?
faqs.a: You have 30 days after receiving written notice of valuation to file a written protest with the County Board of Equalization.

faqs.q: How many people live in Tallapoosa County?
faqs.a: The 2020 census counted 41,311 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 40,953.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Tallapoosa County house with back taxes owed?
faqs.a: Yes. The balance is normally paid out of the sale proceeds at closing, so get a payoff figure from the Revenue Commissioner's office first.
